one_liner: Header-only constexpr C++17 small-state PRNG engines (RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192 and others) with a game-oriented Random<E> API, faster than std::mt19937.
what_it_does: Packages ten small-state engines (4-32 bytes): PCG32, xoshiro256**, Bob Jenkins' SmallFast 8/16/32/64, RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192 and XorShift32Star8, ported to constexpr C++17. Each engine meets UniformRandomBitGenerator, so it works with std::shuffle and std::*_distribution. A Random<E> wrapper adds unbiased bounded integers, floats, coin flips, weighted picks, element selection and an Irwin-Hall approximate normal, plus portable state snapshots (state()/from_state()) for replays. Each engine is seeded from a single uint64_t. It is not a drop-in for std::mt19937's output sequence.
how_it_is_fast: The gain comes from replacing the 624-word Mersenne Twister with register-sized nonlinear generators. RomuDuoJr is one multiply plus a rotate-subtract on two 64-bit words. QuarkBurst64 is rotate/XOR/add with a Weyl counter and no multiply. Konadare192 is add/rotate with a Weyl increment. The wrapper uses Lemire's nearly divisionless multiply-and-reject for bounded integers (division-free when the bound is a compile-time constant). Floats are built by writing random bits into the mantissa field (the 'IQ float hack') instead of dividing.
when_to_use: Games and procedural generation that need fast, reproducible, cross-platform integer streams and replay checkpoints from a tiny state
Many independent generator instances (per entity, per thread, per job) where std::mt19937's 2.5 KiB state is a cache cost
Compile-time generation of tables or test data (engines and most of Random<E> are constexpr)
Bounded integers and weighted picks in hot loops: Lemire's multiply-and-reject avoids most divisions (the README's bounded-integer chart compares it with std::uniform_int_distribution and rand() % n)
8/16-bit microcontrollers (AVR Arduino built as C++17) via the SmallFast8/16 and XorShift32Star8 engines
when_not_to_use: Security or anything adversarial: none of the engines is cryptographic, as the README states

Scientific Monte Carlo that needs proven period, jump-ahead or guaranteed non-overlapping parallel streams: RomuDuoJr has no proven period (its seeding comment cites only empirical cycle checks), and child() explicitly 'does not promise independent or non-overlapping streams'
Code that must reproduce std::mt19937 sequences or the exact output of std distributions

Projects that need high-precision floats by default: normalized()/between() default to float with 23 random mantissa bits, and normal_approx() is an Irwin-Hall approximation clipped at about six standard deviations

When you need audited statistical quality for QuarkBurst64: the repo has known-answer tests against an archived reference but no PractRand/TestU01 results, and the upstream eightomic/quarkburst repo returns 404

integration.form: header-only (copy include/ or link the CMake INTERFACE target cpp_prngs::cpp_prngs)
integration.dependencies: none (GoogleTest is fetched only for the test build)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (CMake 3.21+ for the provided target); C++20 adds constexpr std::bit_cast floats and the rnd::RandomBitEngine concept; AVR needs -std=gnu++17 (CI uses Arduino AVR core 1.8.8)
integration.platforms: any C++17 target (desktop, MSVC project included, AVR Arduino validated in CI)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; engines and Random<E> are plain value types with no global state, so use one instance per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the engines satisfy UniformRandomBitGenerator and can replace std::mt19937 as the engine for std::shuffle or std distributions, but the sequences differ, seeding takes a single uint64_t rather than a seed_seq, and the Random<E> API is its own interface

gotchas: Default construction uses a fixed seed, so Random<E>() gives the same sequence every run. Seeding helpers live in a separate gist (seeding.hpp), not in the repo.

Floating between(lo, hi) is computed as lo + (hi - lo) * normalized(), so rounding can return hi for some ranges despite the documented [lo, hi). In C++17 the float path is constexpr arithmetic unless RND_FAST_FLOAT is defined.
from_state() bypasses seeding. All-zero states are invalid for most engines (PCG32's inc must be odd), and this is checked only by assert in debug builds.

Third-party engine headers keep their own licenses (PCG32 and Konadare192 are Apache-2.0, QuarkBurst's upstream is BSD-3-Clause), so check the per-file headers when vendoring rather than assuming MIT throughout.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cpp_prngs over libchaos or the bare Romu entry when you want ready-to-copy constexpr C++17 engines plus a convenience layer (bounded ints, weighted picks, snapshots) with portable, deterministic output, including on AVR. For SIMD bulk throughput (simdrng, SHISHUA) or scientific-grade streams with jump-ahead (Randen, xoshiro reference code, OpenRAND), look at those entries instead.
verified_claims_summary: The author's Quick Bench charts (August 2026) put raw next() at about 13,300 for std::mt19937 versus about 2,700 for RomuDuoJr and 2,600 for QuarkBurst64, in units of CPU time / no-op time, values read by eye. That is roughly 5x per call, but it compares 64-bit-output engines with the 32-bit-output std::mt19937. Compiler, flags, standard library and CPU are not stated (the Quick Bench links were unreachable). The harness is public (benchmarks/engine_comparison.cpp, Google Benchmark, 1024 values summed per iteration).
status_note: Actively maintained by a single author (232 commits, last 2026-08-20, 1 star, CI on desktop and AVR). MIT for the wrappers, with third-party engines under their original permissive licenses; small enough to vendor.
